history.title: Watch the Sky

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

The sky looks different in the morning than it does at bedtime. This week you find out why — and the answer is not what most people guess.

1. Read **Day Sky, Night Sky** with a grown-up or a partner.
2. Learn the words in **Sky Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Look at the **What the Sky Does** chart.
4. Play **True or Not True?** and put each card in the right pile.
5. Take **Sky Check** — say each answer out loud before you pick it.
6. Lock the big idea in with **Remember Why the Sky Changes**.
7. Read **Sky Questions Kids Ask** if you are wondering about something.
8. Finish with **Investigation: The Shadow Watch** — go outside and find out for yourself.

Your job this week: look up at least once in the morning and once at night, and tell someone one thing you saw. ☀️🌙

Picture panels: Earth turns; Patterns we observe; Sunlight and moonlight; Watch and record. Paper collage pictures are illustrative, not scale drawings or exact maps. Diagram arrows show light paths or turning; they are not solid beams or orbital paths. The Sun stays fixed only in this simplified daily-rotation model, not absolutely still in space. Left-to-right horizon panels represent apparent sky motion as Earth turns. Stars remain in space during daytime; they are usually hidden by bright sky. A Moon picture does not imply it is visible every night. Shadow panels show possible changes, not a guaranteed direction or length. Never look directly at the Sun.

history.title: Day Sky, Night Sky
history.data:
## Day Sky, Night Sky

Look up in the morning. The sky is blue and bright. Look up at bedtime. The sky is dark. Why does the sky change?

Here is the secret. **Earth** is turning. Our whole planet goes around and around, like a very slow top. It makes one full **spin** every day.

When your side of Earth faces the **Sun**, you have **day**. The sky is bright. When your side turns away, you have **night**. The sky goes dark.

So the Sun does not really walk across the sky. You are the one who is moving! Earth turns you toward the Sun at **sunrise**. Later it turns you away at **sunset**.

The Sun is a **star**. It looks big and bright because it is much closer to us than the other stars are. Those far stars do not leave in the morning. They are still up there. The bright blue sky just hides them.

At night you may see the **Moon**. The Moon does not make its own light. Light from the Sun lands on it and bounces to your eyes. That is why it glows.

Here is a surprise. You can see the Moon in the daytime too! Look for a pale white curve up in the blue.

Day, night, day, night. It goes in the same order every time. That is a **pattern**. A pattern lets you guess what comes next.

data.title: Remember Why the Sky Changes
data.instructions: Two cards hold the big ideas from Day Sky, Night Sky. Look at the example, make one your own, then say out loud how it helps you remember.
data.sourceExcerpt: Our whole planet goes around and around, like a very slow top. When your side of Earth faces the Sun, you have day. When your side turns away, you have night. The Moon does not make its own light. Light from the Sun lands on it and bounces to your eyes.

cards.target: Earth turns, and that is what makes day and night
essentialFacts: Earth makes one full spin every day.
When your side faces the Sun it is day.
When your side turns away it is night.
The Sun is not the one moving across the sky.
cards.aiExample: Stand up and turn around slowly. Face the lamp and say 'day.' Keep turning until the lamp is behind you and say 'night.' You moved. The lamp never did.
cards.mapping: Your body is Earth. The lamp is the Sun. Turning your own body shows that the change comes from you, not from the light going anywhere.
cards.scaffoldStarter: I turn toward the lamp: ____. I turn away from the lamp: ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick something bright to be the Sun.
Turn your body all the way around one time.
Say 'day' and 'night' at the right moments.
coachPrompts: In your turn, what moved: you or the lamp?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own turning motion for day and night.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does turning your body help you remember why the sky changes?

hookFact.text: The Sun does not really walk across the sky. You are the one who is moving.

cards.target: The Moon shines with light it borrows from the Sun
essentialFacts: The Moon does not make its own light.
Light from the Sun lands on the Moon and bounces to your eyes.
The Moon can sometimes be seen in the daytime.
cards.aiExample: Picture a mirror on a wall. A mirror is not a lamp. But it can still fill a room with light, because light bounces off it. The Moon is the mirror. The Sun is the lamp.
cards.mapping: Every kid has watched a mirror bounce light. So it carries the one idea that matters. The Moon is bright without being a light of its own.
cards.scaffoldStarter: The Moon is like a ____, and the Sun is like a ____.
scaffoldSteps: Think of something shiny that has no light inside it.
Say where its light comes from.
Say the same thing about the Moon.
coachPrompts: If the Sun went out, what would happen to the Moon's glow?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own picture for a thing that shines with borrowed light.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why is a mirror a better match for the Moon than a candle is?

history.meta: 2 piles • 8 cards • four of them are the guesses kids usually make

questions.question: What makes day turn into night?
options: The Sun flies away to another sky
Earth spins, and your side turns away
Clouds cover the Sun until morning
The Sun turns off its light at bedtime
questions.correctAnswer: Earth spins, and your side turns away

questions.question: The Sun is really a ______.
options: cloud that glows in the daytime
very big fire we lit long ago
star that is close to us
hole in the sky letting light in
questions.correctAnswer: star that is close to us

questions.question: Where are the stars in the middle of the day?
options: Still in the sky, hidden by the bright blue
Gone away until the sky gets dark again
Sleeping behind the Moon until night
Falling down to the ground each morning
questions.correctAnswer: Still in the sky, hidden by the bright blue

questions.question: Why does the Moon glow?
options: It is a small hot star of its own
It burns a fire deep inside itself
It catches light from the streets below
Sunlight lands on it and bounces to us
questions.correctAnswer: Sunlight lands on it and bounces to us

questions.question: You see a pale white Moon in a blue afternoon sky. What is going on?
options: Something is wrong; the Moon has lost its way
That can happen; the Moon is up in the daytime too
It must be a cloud, because the Moon comes only at night
The sky is getting ready to turn dark much too early
questions.correctAnswer: That can happen; the Moon is up in the daytime too

questions.question: Tell what Earth does to make day and night.
questions.expectedAnswer: Earth spins all the way around one time each day. When your side faces the Sun it is day, and when your side turns away it is night.

questions.question: Your friend says the stars go away every morning. What would you tell them?
questions.expectedAnswer: The stars do not go away. They are still up in the sky, but the daytime sky is so bright that it hides them until it gets dark again.

history.title: Sky Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Can I feel Earth spinning? 🌍
data.answer: No, and that is the strange part. Everything near you turns at the same speed you do. The ground. The air. The trees. Your chair. Nothing gets left behind, so there is nothing to feel.

data.question: Is the Sun bigger than the other stars? ☀️
data.answer: It is bigger than most stars, and much smaller than some. It only looks huge because it is so close. Hold a coin near your eye. It can block a whole building.

data.question: Why is the sky blue in the daytime? 💙
data.answer: Sunlight is made of many colors mixed together. The air bounces the blue part all over the sky. So blue comes at you from every side.

data.question: Does the Moon change shape? 🌙
data.answer: The Moon stays the same round rock. What changes is how much of its sunny side you can see. That is why it looks like a curve some nights and a full circle on others.

data.question: Why can I sometimes see the Moon at lunchtime?
data.answer: Because the Moon is up in the sky then. It is bright enough to show through the blue. Look on a clear afternoon and see if you can spot it.

data.question: Is it night everywhere at the same time?
data.answer: No. When it is night where you are, your side of Earth faces away from the Sun. The other side is having its day. Someone far away eats lunch while you sleep.

history.title: Investigation: The Shadow Watch
history.meta: 1st Grade • Investigation brief • one chalk mark, three times

data.title: The Shadow Watch
data.instructions: Stand in the same spot three times in one day and trace your shadow with chalk. Guess first what will happen, then find out.
data.fitReason: The lesson says Earth turns, but a first grader cannot feel it. A shadow that moves and changes size across one day is the evidence they can see with their own eyes, which is exactly what the standard asks for: observe a pattern that can be predicted.

brief.context: Your class has sidewalk chalk and a sunny paved spot outside. You can go out three times in one day: morning, the middle of the day, and late afternoon.
brief.audience: The kindergarten class, who will come outside to look at your chalk marks
brief.drivingQuestion: Stand in the very same spot three times in one day. Will your shadow stay in the same place? Will it stay the same size?
brief.seedDirection: Stand on the same X every time. If you move your feet, you will not know if the shadow moved or you did.
lockedLessonFacts: Earth makes one full spin every day.
Earth turns you toward the Sun at sunrise and away from it at sunset.
The Sun is not the thing that moves across the sky.
Day and night come in the same order every time, which makes a pattern.
openQuestions: Will your shadow be longer in the morning, or in the middle of the day?
Which way will your shadow point when you come back out?
How will you make sure you stand in the same place each time?
stakeholders: The kindergarten class who will visit your marks
Your partner who traces while you stand still
The teacher who takes you outside on time
criteria: Your feet are on the same chalk X all three times
You draw or say your guess before the first tracing
Each shadow is traced, with the time of day on it
You use the word pattern or the word spin when you tell what happened
constraints: Nobody looks straight at the Sun
brief.deliverable: A chalk drawing on the ground. Three traced shadows, each with its time. And one sentence you tell the visiting class: what changed, and why.

parallelExample.context: A student wanted to know if a flagpole's shadow moved.
parallelExample.move: He put a rock at the tip of the flagpole shadow before school and a second rock at the tip after lunch, then walked the distance between the two rocks and counted eleven steps.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: He left the flagpole alone and marked only the shadow, so the eleven steps could not be anything except the shadow moving.

supports.frameStarter: In the morning my shadow was ____. Later it was ____. It changed because Earth ____.
frameChoices: short and close to my feet
coachPrompts: Did you stand on the same X every time?
What did your shadow do that surprised you?
Was the Sun moving, or were you?
